statuses.label: German, EU, EEA or Swiss citizen
statuses.headline: No permit test applies to you.
statuses.detail: Living in Germany is enough under section 62 (1) of the Income Tax Act. If you work here while your children live in another EU country, you can still claim, and the other country's family benefit is set against it.

statuses.label: Settlement permit or EU long-term residence permit
statuses.headline: A Niederlassungserlaubnis settles it.
statuses.detail: Section 62 (2) names the Niederlassungserlaubnis and the Erlaubnis zum Daueraufenthalt-EU first. Nothing else has to be proved.

statuses.label: A residence permit that lets you work (Blue Card, skilled worker, family reunion with work access)
statuses.headline: A work-bearing permit normally qualifies.
statuses.detail: Section 62 (2) covers permits that allow employment, with a short list of exceptions. Read the exceptions in the law before you assume, and keep the permit page that shows the work permission.

statuses.label: Study, training, au pair, voluntary service or job-seeking permit
statuses.headline: The permit alone does not do it.
statuses.detail: Permits under sections 16b, 16d, 16e, 19c, 19e, 20 and 20a (5) of the Residence Act are named as exceptions. You still qualify if you are actually employed or self-employed, on Elternzeit, or drawing benefits under Book III of the Social Code.

statuses.label: Humanitarian permit under section 23 (1), 23a or 25 (3) to (5)
statuses.headline: There is a fifteen-month clock on top.
statuses.detail: For these permits section 62 (2) asks for fifteen months of lawful, permitted or tolerated residence in Germany, unless you are working, on Elternzeit or drawing Book III benefits, in which case it starts earlier.
